content.comment:
Interesting work! We've worked on similar problems using variational models: Variational Sequential Labelers for Semi-Supervised Learning (EMNLP 2018), although we didn't consider CRF.

It would be nice if authors could describe the differences in the paper.
content.title: missing related work?

content.comment:
Thank you for your interest and the reference! 

We were previously unaware of this work but, yes, it's definitely related and we will happily add a discussion of its relevance and reference to the paper.

On the differences between this paper and " Variational Sequential Labelers for Semi-Supervised Learning (EMNLP 2018)" (referred to as VSL):

Overall, the papers both approach semi-supervised learning for tagging by adding an unsupervised VAE-like objective, but the specifics of  the model architectures, objective formulations, and evaluations actually all differ quite substantially.

**TL;DR:** Our method uses globally-normalized, discrete sequences for latent variables while VSL uses per-timestep latent gaussians. Because of this, the prior distributions and model architectures differ substantially (see below). Our method focuses on the advantages of unrestrictive generative factorizations while VSL focuses on the structure of latent variables. The evaluations are not directly comparable because they use different datasets -- a comparison of the methods would certainly be interesting and we are willing to add this. Finally, our method addresses a realistic "partial supervision" scenario that VSL does not.


** (1) Modeling objective: **

The VSL paper defines the modeling objective to be "predict a token in the sentence, given all other tokens, using a pair of continuous latent variables as the bottleneck".  A quote directly from the VSL paper: "Unlike VAEs, VSLs do not autoencode the input, so they are more similar to recent conditional variational formulations".

This is quite different than our model. 

1. We first note that we do autoencode the entire input sequence x_{1:N} with a full sequence of latent variables y_{1:N} (i.e., p(x_{1:N}|y_{1:N})). This is more in line with a typical generative model, while the VSL paper _generative model_ is more like the BERT single-token objective conditioning on single latent "tag" information. Indeed, a major contribution of our work is showing that tagging performance can be improved using joint decoding of x_{1:N} given the full tag sequence y_{1:N} instead of a factored model. I.e., p(x_{1:N}|y_{1:N}) instead of \prod_{t} p(x_t|y_t) 

2. The latent variables y_t and z_t used in VSL are **both continuous** Gaussian distributed vectors and supervision is imparted via a multitask objective on another model for predicting tags p(l_t|y_t).  In stark contrast, our method uses the **discrete** tags y_{1:N} as the only latent variables and supervision is imparted directly on the approximate posterior, because it is the same model as the tagger.

3. In VSL, the prior is defined to be the previous posterior estimate as a learned prior. In our work, because the latent variables are discrete, we manually set the prior to be a rudimentary informed per-tag categorical distribution, placing 50% mass on the O tag and evenly distributing the remaining mass to the other tasks. We view the discrete prior as an advantage since we are able use it to impart knowledge on the model -- this is key to addressing the more difficult "partially supervised" setting.


** (2) Model Architectures: **

Our tagging model uses state-of-the-art pretrained language model encodings, a learned transformer layer, and a globally normalized linear-chain CRF for decoding tag sequences jointly, whereas VSL uses a Bi-GRU to encode the tokens represented with pretrained word vectors.  For generation, VSL uses a feed-forward NN, whereas we use a transformer architecture.

Another major contribution of our work is that we are able use a powerful joint-decoding transformer with globally normalized latent tag sequences by adapting Relaxed Perturb-and-MAP to linear chain CRFs. In VSL, locally normalized continuous latent variables are used to make learning tractable via the reparameterization trick for Gaussians.

** (3) Evaluation: **

The evaluation goals of the two works differ substantially. VSL focuses on exploring variation in the hierarchy structure of the two latent variables, always generating tokens with a per-timestep factorization p(x_t|y_t,x_t) parameterized with a feed-forward NN. We instead keep the latent structure fixed as discrete tag sequences and focus on exploring different parameterizations of the generative model p(x_{1:N}|y_{1:N}).

For experiments, VSL evaluates on more datasets (7 POS datasets, the CoNLL03 NER dataset) while we focus on the more difficult Ontonotes5 NER dataset. Our results show net larger increases in F1 score by adding unlabeled data in the 10% labeled data regime (+0.9-1.3 F1 vs. +0.1-0.3F1), but they are not directly comparable to VSL because the datasets and setups used differ.

Another major difference is that we contribute a method for learning in a realistic and more difficult "Partial Supervision" regime where individual annotations are missing from sentences and there are no labeled O tags. This challenge is not addressed by VSL.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This work applies CRF autoencoder to the task of semi-supervised named entity recognition. The latent variables are the discrete tag sequences; and to facilitate end-to-end training, an amortized variational objective is used. Different generative model (i.e., generating input tokens conditioning on the latent tags)   architectures are explored. Experiments with NER with the Ontonotes 5 dataset show that, with proper architectures and prior distribution, the proposed model outperforms strong baselines. 

Overall I find the paper clearly presented and well executed. However there is not much to learn from the technical part: most of the key components have been around for a while, and the paper does not seem to attempt to solve any key challenges.

To be more constructive, I think the paper can be improved by:

- Evaluating the proposed method with other tagging tasks, and discuss whether the architecture and prior distribution choices for the generative model are task-dependent. 

- Discussing how the model (especially the generative part) translate to other structured latent variables, e.g., syntactic trees and semantic graphs.

- More carefully evaluating the partially supervised learning objective, which seems interesting can could potentially benefit future research.

I'm happy to adjust the score if the authors can justify the technical contribution and take the effort to improve the paper.

content.title: Response to Review #1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments. 

We agree that moving technical details of model implementations in sections 2.2 and 2.4 to the appendix while bringing the discussion of relaxed perturb-and-map for linear-chain crfs and the derivation of the generalized forward-backward algorithm from the appendices A and B would better highlight and clarify the novel elements of our work.

- Evaluate on other tasks:
We agree, this model framework is more general to (at least) tagging and we will add comparisons on more datasets to see if our results are task-dependent.

- Discuss how the model translates to other structured latent variables:
We think this is a very interesting direction for future work, but we haven’t explored it yet.

- More carefully evaluate the partially supervised objective:
We again agree that this is an interesting direction for future work. Perhaps some sort of active-learning experiment could demonstrate the practical value of the partially supervised objective.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper considers the task of Named Entity Recognition and formulates it as a the task of segmenting a sequence of text tokens by a corresponding sequence of tags. This requires to use a special tag symbol which is labelling text parts that are not in any entity span. Consequently this special tag will never occur in partially annotated training examples. Moreover, the authors consider and explore a multitude of generative models whose decoders (conditional probability of the text sequence given the tag sequence) are beyond simple conditional independent models (as in standard HMMs). To learn such models from semi-supervised and partially labelled training data, the authors propose to use the VAE approach, assuming the encoder to be a linear CRF model (i.e. a conditional HMM). Implementing this program requires (i) to formulate the tasks for unlabelled and partially labelled training data, (2) to use an approximate but differentiable sampler for the encoder model and (3) to compute the KL-divergence for Markov chain models. The authors consider known options for each of these problems and then analyse the resulting approach for a multitude of generative models experimentally. 

In my opinion the task formulation, the related models and considered learning tasks are highly interesting and conceptually relevant. Nevertheless, I would not recommend to publish the paper in its present state for the following reasons. The paper is in my view to much application oriented and cluttered with various application/implementation details, which are rather obscuring several interesting and relevant conceptual questions. The same holds in my view for the  unnecessary large number of considered model variants. The paper can be improved by moving the conceptual and technical explanations from appendices to the main body and delegating application details, details of some model variants etc. to the appendices. 

Further questions/comments:
- Why are you using a fully factorising prior for the tag sequences? Would it be possible to use a Markov chain model here?
- Why and where from comes the log probability of the encoder (q) in the supervised loss?
- The score function estimation and other similar approaches indeed suffer from high variance gradients. On the other hand, the proposed relaxed "perturb and MAP" approach is clearly an approximation. It is therefore not clear to me why the latter is to be preferred to the former.

content.title: Response to Review #3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments. We agree that moving technical details of model implementations in sections 2.2 and 2.4 to the appendix while bringing the discussion of relaxed perturb-and-map for linear-chain crfs and the derivation of the generalized forward-backward algorithm from the appendices A and B would better highlight and clarify the novel elements of our work.

* Why fully factored prior? Why not MRF?
We agree, it would be interesting to try an MRF prior distribution, but it’s unclear that it would really improve performance. An unconditional linear-chain MRF would still distribute mass relatively uniformly over the space of all sequences, remaining considerably higher entropy than the inference CRF and so we’d likely still need to heavily down-weigh the KL term.

* Why and where does the supervised logq term come from? 
This is an additional supervised loss, separate from the variational bound that we have added. It promotes q learning from all possible observations, and is typical in SSL VAEs (see e.g., [1] “Semi-supervised learning with deep generative models”, Kingma et al. 14)

* It’s not obvious that score-function is worse than perturb-and-map. 
We again agree, we do not (and little work out there does) compare unbiased but high-variance score-function with biased but lower-variance gumbel-softmax, especially for structured prediction. We think this would be a useful additional experiment and will add to future work.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper treats the CRF-based NER tagger as the amortized variational posterior in a generative model of text given tags. In this manner, a VAE is defined that can be trained in a semi-supervised manner. Partially supervised learning (PSL) is also explored.

This paper is not well-written for the following reasons.

1. This paper over-claims:  "to our knowledge, we are the first to utilize VAEs for NER." 

There are some works in applying VAEs to sequence labelling, even the harder seq2seq learning. For example,

[a] Language as a latent variable: Discrete generative models for sentence compression, EMNLP 2016.
[b] StructVAE: Tree-structured Latent Variable Models for Semi-supervised Semantic Parsing, ACL 2018.

The authors should concentrate on the novel elements of their proposed method. A straightforward of applying VAEs to NER for semi-supervised learning does not warrant an publication at ICLR.

2. Unfortunately, the novel elements are not elaborated. It is difficult for the reader to tell which parts of the proposed method are novel.
If only looking at the technical development in the main paper (without the Appendices), the development seems to be weak, not substantial contribution from applying VAEs. The authors should make a better balance between the main content and the Appendices.

3. The experimental results are also not well organized. Comparisons are here and there, without a main thread.
MF, MT are used without definitions.

content.title: Response to Review #2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comments. 

1. The paper over-claims:
We did not intend to over-claim and are willing to remove that statement. Although there are prior works using seq2seq in VAEs, they use locally normalized models which do not require sampling from and computing KLs for globally normalized linear-chain CRFs. 

2. Novel elements need to be elaborated: 
We agree that moving technical details of model implementations in sections 2.2 and 2.4 to the appendix while bringing the discussion of relaxed perturb-and-map for linear-chain crfs and the derivation of the generalized forward-backward algorithm from the appendices A and B would better highlight and clarify the novel elements of our work.

3. Experiments are not well-organized. Comparisons are here and there, without a main thread. MF, MT are not defined:
We apologize if the experimental narrative is unclear. We believe these experiments show that:
  1. A transformer decoder, enabled by our relaxed perturb-and-map approach provides significant gains (>1% absolute F1) in performance over strong prior approaches in a moderate-resource setting (10% labeled data)
  2. The use of a prior further improves performance and aptly addresses the degenerate partially-supervised scenario
  3. Our model additionally provides similar benefits in a low-resource regime (1% labeled data) but does not provide the same gains when there is enough (100%) labeled data.
Both experiments (2) and (3) build off the results of (1).

MF and MT are defined in Section 2.4.
